text: Rule DCLAB-R01 (problem_contract): Write the prediction moment, target window, action, unit of prediction and error costs before inspecting target associations. Why: Leakage is defined relative to what is knowable at a specific decision moment, not by a column name. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Write the prediction moment, target window, action, unit of prediction and error costs before inspecting target associations.

text: Rule DCLAB-R02 (splitting): Split by the real independence unit and time direction before preprocessing or feature selection. Why: Random rows leak entity history and future regimes when observations are related. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Split by the real independence unit and time direction before preprocessing or feature selection.

text: Rule DCLAB-R03 (eda): Fit target-aware EDA, imputers, encoders, scalers, selectors and learned aggregations on training partitions only. Why: Any statistic that sees evaluation labels or distributions can make validation optimistic. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Fit target-aware EDA, imputers, encoders, scalers, selectors and learned aggregations on training partitions only.

text: Rule DCLAB-R04 (leakage): Treat post-outcome, future, target-derived, cross-split aggregate, duplicate/entity and preprocessing leakage as separate failure modes. Why: One correlation detector cannot identify all leakage mechanisms. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Treat post-outcome, future, target-derived, cross-split aggregate, duplicate/entity and preprocessing leakage as separate failure modes.

text: Rule DCLAB-R05 (leakage): A suspicious name or high univariate AUC starts a semantic review; it does not prove leakage. Why: Availability requires source lineage and timestamps; useful real predictors can also be highly associated. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: A suspicious name or high univariate AUC starts a semantic review; it does not prove leakage.

text: Rule DCLAB-R06 (leakage): A large safe-versus-unsafe score gap is a severity demonstration, not the primary proof of leakage. Why: Bank marketing and online shoppers showed +0.1328 to +0.1575 registry gaps, while semantics identified the forbidden fields. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: strong empirical.
title: A large safe-versus-unsafe score gap is a severity demonstration, not the primary proof of leakage.

text: Rule DCLAB-R07 (feature_engineering): Begin with a strong raw baseline and promote the smallest defensible feature set within a predeclared tolerance. Why: Seven of ten campaign datasets selected raw features; extra features often added dilution without repeatable lift. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: moderate empirical.
title: Begin with a strong raw baseline and promote the smallest defensible feature set within a predeclared tolerance.

text: Rule DCLAB-R08 (feature_engineering): Generate features from domain invariances and mechanisms before blind combinatorial expansion. Why: Ratios helped bank marketing and wine quality; interactions helped German credit; churn charge/tenure features improved logistic AUC by +0.0050. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: moderate empirical.
title: Generate features from domain invariances and mechanisms before blind combinatorial expansion.

text: Rule DCLAB-R09 (feature_engineering): Every generated feature needs explicit lineage, availability time, units, null behavior and a reproducible formula. Why: A mathematically valid feature can still be unavailable, unstable or impossible to reproduce online. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Every generated feature needs explicit lineage, availability time, units, null behavior and a reproducible formula.

text: Rule DCLAB-R10 (feature_reliability): Importance is only a nomination signal; production reliability additionally requires availability, fold stability, coverage, missing-input resilience and drift monitoring. Why: The campaign explicitly rejects importance-only promotion and the agentic worker measures missing-input stress. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Importance is only a nomination signal; production reliability additionally requires availability, fold stability, coverage, missing-input resilience and drift monitoring.

text: Rule DCLAB-R11 (categoricals): Preserve raw categorical semantics and fit encoders inside folds; do not treat arbitrary category codes as ordered numbers. Why: Legacy factorized caches lose labels and can introduce false ordinal structure. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Preserve raw categorical semantics and fit encoders inside folds; do not treat arbitrary category codes as ordered numbers.

text: Rule DCLAB-R12 (missingness): Model missingness as an operational state: measure coverage, add indicators when justified, simulate absence, and define fallback behavior. Why: A feature that disappears in production can dominate offline ranking yet make the system brittle. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Model missingness as an operational state: measure coverage, add indicators when justified, simulate absence, and define fallback behavior.

text: Rule DCLAB-R14 (model_selection): Use mean performance, fold stability, probability quality, runtime and operational constraints—not ROC-AUC alone. Why: Small AUC wins can coincide with worse log loss, calibration, recall or latency. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Use mean performance, fold stability, probability quality, runtime and operational constraints—not ROC-AUC alone.

text: Rule DCLAB-R15 (optimization): Optimize only after data, leakage, features, metric and candidate family are locked. Why: Early broad tuning increases adaptive overfitting and obscures what caused improvement. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Optimize only after data, leakage, features, metric and candidate family are locked.

text: Rule DCLAB-R16 (optimization): Compare tuning and feature changes with a paired baseline on the same folds and demand a predeclared useful margin. Why: The campaign used a 0.001 CV gate; this is a project convention, not a universal constant. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Compare tuning and feature changes with a paired baseline on the same folds and demand a predeclared useful margin.

text: Rule DCLAB-R17 (evaluation): Consume the final holdout once, after all choices are locked, and never tune from its result. Why: Repeated consultation converts a holdout into development data. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Consume the final holdout once, after all choices are locked, and never tune from its result.

text: Rule DCLAB-R18 (evaluation): Choose metrics and thresholds from the real decision cost; report ranking, probability quality and operating-point errors together. Why: AUC does not specify calibration or the false-positive/false-negative tradeoff. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Choose metrics and thresholds from the real decision cost; report ranking, probability quality and operating-point errors together.

text: Rule DCLAB-R19 (generalization): Use temporal, geographic, source-system and out-of-domain slices when those shifts exist. Why: Random CV estimates interpolation under the historical mixture, not future operational performance. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Use temporal, geographic, source-system and out-of-domain slices when those shifts exist.

text: Rule DCLAB-R20 (llm_governance): Let LLM agents propose hypotheses, challenge semantics and curate cited lessons; deterministic executors own splits, metrics and artifacts. Why: This preserves creativity without letting generated text become measurement. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high system-design.
title: Let LLM agents propose hypotheses, challenge semantics and curate cited lessons; deterministic executors own splits, metrics and artifacts.

text: Rule DCLAB-R21 (knowledge): Store claims with scope, evidence IDs, counterevidence, uncertainty and the next discriminating test. Why: A score without context cannot teach a future person or model when the lesson applies. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: Store claims with scope, evidence IDs, counterevidence, uncertainty and the next discriminating test.

text: Rule DCLAB-R22 (promotion): A candidate is not production-ready until provenance, independent confirmation, feature contracts, monitoring, fairness/privacy and rollback gates are reviewed. Why: Benchmark excellence does not establish operational safety. Failure signal: The result changes materially under a valid ablation, later-time slice, missing-input simulation, or independent evaluation. Next test: Record the decision and test it on identical folds. Confidence: high methodological.
title: A candidate is not production-ready until provenance, independent confirmation, feature contracts, monitoring, fairness/privacy and rollback gates are reviewed.

text: Pitfall experiment PIT-001: How much does fitting an imputer and scaler on all rows before the train/test split inflate the holdout score? Setup: Logistic regression with mean imputation + standard scaling on 6 datasets (≤8000 rows each), 3 random stratified 80/20 splits; wrong = preprocessing fitted on all rows, right = fitted on training rows only. Findings: Fitting mean-imputation and scaling before the split changed holdout ROC-AUC by at most 0.0001 on average (german_credit). Still fit every preprocessing step inside the training data (a Pipeline): the measured cost is small here, but the identical mistake with feature selection, oversampling or target encoding is large (PIT-002, PIT-003, PIT-004). Limitations: Simple, unsupervised, row-wise transforms only; learned or target-aware transforms behave very differently.
title: PIT-001 · measured cost of: preprocess before split

text: Pitfall experiment PIT-002: How much does selecting features on all rows before cross-validation inflate the CV score? Setup: SelectKBest(f_classif) + logistic regression, 5-fold CV, 3 seeds. A pure-noise canary (random labels, 2000 features, 200 rows) plus three real datasets (≤4000 rows). Wrong = selection fitted once on all rows; right = selection inside each training fold. Findings: On pure noise with random labels, selecting 20 of 2000 features before CV produced ROC-AUC 0.859; doing it inside the folds gave 0.512 (chance is 0.5). On the real datasets (few features, thousands of rows) the inflation was at most +0.0041. Put feature selection inside the cross-validated pipeline. The danger grows with the number of candidate features relative to rows, so wide data (text, genomics, many engineered features) is where this mistake fabricates results. Limitations: Univariate filter selection only; wrapper/model-based selection can inflate more.
title: PIT-002 · measured cost of: selection before cv

text: Pitfall experiment PIT-003: How much does oversampling the minority class before the split inflate the holdout score? Setup: Random minority oversampling to a 50/50 balance, random forest (200 trees), 4 imbalanced datasets (≤6000 rows), 3 seeds. Wrong = oversample then split; right = split, oversample the training rows only. Findings: Oversampling before the split inflated holdout ROC-AUC by up to +0.3003 on average (online_shoppers: 0.9019 reported vs 0.6016 honest). Resample only inside the training data (imblearn Pipeline or after the split), and evaluate on untouched, naturally imbalanced rows with a metric that respects imbalance such as average precision. Limitations: Random duplication oversampling; SMOTE interpolates new points and leaks through near-duplicates instead of exact copies.
title: PIT-003 · measured cost of: oversample before split

text: Pitfall experiment PIT-006: If we pick the best of many configurations by their holdout score, how optimistic is that holdout score? Setup: 30 random LightGBM configurations per run on a 60/20/20 split into train and two holdouts, 5 datasets (≤6000 rows), 3 seeds, both selection directions. Bias = the picked model's score drop from the selection holdout to the untouched one, minus the average drop across all configurations. Findings: Choosing the best of 30 configurations by holdout score overstated ROC-AUC by +0.0072 on average and by +0.0177 on german_credit; on the untouched holdout the pick ranked 7.2 of 30 on average. Tune with cross-validation on training data, then touch the holdout once. If the holdout was used to choose, the reported score is biased upward; confirm on a fresh split or use nested CV. The bias grows with the number of configurations tried and shrinks with holdout size. Limitations: Configurations from one model family are highly correlated, which keeps the bias small; comparing many unrelated pipelines inflates more.
title: PIT-006 · measured cost of: holdout reuse for selection

text: Pitfall experiment PIK-001 on the binary kind: On the Binary classification replica, how much better does a wrong split or a kept leak make the score look? Setup: 3 seeds of the binary replica; 20% held out; histogram gradient boosting with default settings; ROC-AUC; right split: the latest rows by time. Findings: On the Binary classification replica, a random split instead of the latest rows by time showed no difference beyond the spread of 3 seeds (mean 0.0062, 95% interval -0.0315 to 0.0438). On the Binary classification replica, the planted leak kept in makes the ROC-AUC look better by 0.3361 on average over 3 seeds (95% interval 0.2916 to 0.3806). Limitations: Invented replica data with its traps planted, one model family with default settings: the size of the effect on a real table differs; the direction is what the replica shows. No difference measured on this replica: it plants no effect of this kind (no drift over time), which says nothing about a real table, where a random split is still the wrong one for a time-ordered problem.
title: PIK-001 · Binary classification: what its pitfalls cost on its replica
